Then, weight is mass times gravity, so if gravity is slightly less at the top of a mountain, the weight should be a bit less. That makes sense because you might feel lighter when you're at a higher altitude.

Next, body density. Density is mass divided by volume. If gravity is weaker, does that affect the volume? I remember that at higher altitudes, the atmospheric pressure is lower. Since a lot of our body is made up of gas, like in our lungs and the digestive system, lower pressure might cause those gases to expand. Using Boyle's Law, if pressure decreases, volume increases. So if 10% of our body volume is gas, that could expand by about 33%, making the total volume larger. That would make the density (mass/volume) lower because the volume has increased more than the mass has changed. So body density would be less, but the effect is bigger than the change in weight.

Body temperature is probably the same because it's regulated by our metabolism, not directly affected by gravity or altitude. So temperature doesn't change much.
